column2: NWF Oct 2022_Documenting Transitions Through The Gate
column3: Funding towards two projects: Be Rock Solid and Bars to Business. The overarching aim of each project is to prepare, shape and transition offenders from custody into sharing in the whole life of the community . Offenders completing the projects move forward with a mindset, set of tools and new way of thinking that promotes positive aspirations for a future free from the cycle of the criminal justice system. We have had many positive successes from our initial project delivery. Our work has become the focus of the National Young Adults Project Team, looking at how we can help shape strong rehabilitative cultures in prisons and translate this into positive outcomes for young adults leaving custody. Funding from The Wates Foundation will help us tell the stories of these transitions to raise awareness and share our impact amongst the community. Using videography, experiences and written and spoken word of our beneficiaries, we will capture six transitions from prison to community.

5G RuralDorset will deliver the following:Business models for rural 5G servicesWe will address the cost and design challenges of using common wireless infrastructure at national scale to deliver services to rural communities. This will be evaluated by three service providers and across four different test-beds that respond to the needs of those living, working and visiting rural and coastal regions of Dorset and beyond.Rural 5G Testbed rural communities are poorly serviced by wireless connectivity. We will deploy a wide-area 5G wireless testbed allowing businesses and academia to prove the sustainable commercial case for improved 5G connectivity in rural locations. We will deploy new wireless technology on existing masts and fibre owned and operated by internet service provider Wessex Internet allowing rapid deployment on a significant scale. The resulting connectivity will support uses in agriculture and provide access to digital services tackling rural issues including isolation and social care needs. This will show that existing and new infrastructure can be combined to deliver next generation connectivity more affordably.Connected Coast the UKs coastal regions generate significant economic wealth and support a range of leisure activities that boost health and well-being. But the coast can be very dangerous. There are serious challenges communicating in such regions, with the first responder community and organisations including the RNLI, Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) and General Lighthouse Authority (GLA) having very limited access to digital communications services. We will deploy a 5G services test-bed in the Lulworth Cove area and a further maritime safety test-bed on infrastructure along the coast. We will trial digital applications that engage with the public and improve the responsiveness of emergency services to incidents. We will evaluate the upgrade of existing infrastructure around the coast and develop the social and economic case for deployment, considering additional use cases from tourism and aquaculture to education and healthcare.5G Innovation Testbed We will deploy an advanced connectivity testbed at the heart of Dorset Innovation Park, a Local Enterprise Zone and advanced-engineering centre which already supports large and small companies that develop innovative connected products and services. This testbed will be connected to other sites in the UK and focus on wide-area connectivity solutions for rural and coastal regions. It will support businesses operating in the county and across the supply chain to test and develop products before deployment in a collaborative and secure way in this strategically important location.

To support local delivery, the Authority invites the 47 recognised Local Nature Partnerships (LNPs) to bid competitively for funding to explore the best solutions to strengthen their partnership. This measure is the primary Agri-environment-climate funding for England in delivering the Rural Development programme environmental land management priorities and builds on the agri-environment Countryside Stewardship and Environmental Stewardship schemes offered under the previous RD programme.The measure funds activities intended to deliver environmental land management priorities contributing to Englands Biodiversity 2020 goals and legal obligations under the Habitats, Birds and Water Framework Directives and soil commitments made in the Natural Environment White Paper and increase resilience of wildlife, habitats and ecosystems to climate change.Funding is paid according to the payment rate for each option included in the individual agreement, and the area/length/number of the commitment selected and is based on income foregone and additional costs. Agreements can be 5 year multi annual commitments with the option of annual extensions for a further two years. 10 year commitments or longer will be offered in cases where an exception is clearly justified.RPA administers for measures in England.

The Police Transformation Fund (PTF) is a police-led fund which provides PCCs with a real opportunity to transform policing and invest in digitalisation, a diverse and flexible workforce, and new and more efficient capabilities to respond to changing crimes and threats. It aims to incentivise policing to meet future challenges by being more efficient and effective, and build capability to respond to a changing crime mix.Phase 1 of the fund (2016/17 and 2017/18) focused on rapid, relatively low-cost work to deliver early transformation to a set of priority capabilities (e.g. digital intelligence and investigation); funding specific new capabilities (e.g. professionalising the police response to modern slavery); and working with policing partners to develop a broader blueprint for transformation over the course of the Parliament.2018/19 is the start of phase 2 of the fund which will implement the investment priorities developed and set by the Police Reform and Transformation Board (PRTB) during phase 1.

column3: The Green Homes Grant Local Authority Delivery scheme was launched in August 2020. This £500 million scheme funds energy efficiency and low carbon heating projects for low income households across England. It supports delivery of the target to reduce fuel poverty in England, the UKs pathway to net zero by 2050 as well as stimulating the economic recovery following COVID-19, supporting, and creating green jobs. The Local Authority Delivery scheme aims to upgrade around 50,000 homes, saving consumers money on their energy bills, while making it easier to keep their homes warm.The Local Authority Delivery Scheme is being delivered in Phases:- Phase 1A:grants of around £74 million were allocated to 55 projects which aimed to upgrade the energy efficiency of around 10,000 low-income households in over 100 local authorities across all areas in England by the end of August 2021- Phase 1B: around £126 million of funding was allocated to 81 local authorities for delivery of energy efficiency projects by the end of March 2022, aiming to upgrade around 15,000 homes. This included consortium bids submitted by a lead local authority that cover energy efficiency upgrades across multiple geographically related local authorities

The VPRS scheme has been expanded to meet a commitment made by the former Prime Minister, and is being run by a tri-partite team of officials (the Syrian Resettlement Programme) from the the Home Office and the departments for International Development and Communities and Local Government. This team sits within the Resettlement, Asylum Support and Integration Direcorate in UK Visas and Immigration. This team also has responsibility for running the Vulnerable Childrens Resettlement Scheme.As such, this funding is to be used to meet a government commitment, rather than a Home Office strategic priority. Three key objectives have been set for the schemes: resettling Syrian refugees in a way that:Secures and Protects the vulnerable persons and the UK, andHas the Well-being of the vulnerable persons and the welcoming communities at the centre of decision making, andDelivers value for money for the UK tax payer.This grant is primarily designed to assist with promoting refugee well being, whilst ensuring value for money. It is designed to contribute to costs incurred for the first year that beneficiaries spend in the UK for primary and secondary health care costs.The VPR scheme was upscaled in September 2015 to meet commitments made by the former Prime Minister, including to resettle 1,000 Syrians by Christmas 2015. In view of the scale of the challenge and limited time available, the Home Secretary authorised the formation of a Gold Command Structure, which provided the designated Gold Commander (Paul Morrison) with high-level Ministerial authority to make the necessary funding and operational decisions to deliver these commitments. The VCRS scheme was announced in April 2016 and utilises the same delivery partners.Since then the formation of the Gold Command, the Programme  which operates both schemes  has had regular contact with Ministers at Secretary of State level. They are aware of our choice of delivery partners and funding model.The VPR and VCRS schemes are being evaluated through a programme of data monitoring and qualitative research and this will include examining some VFM considerations.

On 7 September 2015 the serving Prime Minister announced the expansion of existing UK resettlement schemes to resettle up to 20,000 Syrian refugees under a new Vulnerable Person Resettlement Scheme (VPRS) by 2020. The scope of this Programme was expanded in July 2017 to include the most vulnerable refugees in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region who have fled the Syrian conflict, regardless of nationality.In April 2016 a further commitment was made to resettle up to 3,000 children and their families from the (MENA) region over the same period under the Children at Risk UNHCR vulnerability category, the Vulnerable Children Resettlement Scheme (VCRS).This grant stream is for the provision of post-arrival services to refugees resettled in the UK under these schemes through tariff/per capita payments.At present the majority of arrivals are being supported by local authorities and the funding provides an un-ringfenced contribution to their costs.Payments may also be made for some local authority services for families resettled under the Community Sponsorship scheme which the Home Secretary announced in July 2016.Payments are also made for the same purpose to Horton Housing Association.The required outcomes include:- The Recipient will arrange accommodation for the arriving Beneficiaries which meets local authority standards, and which will be available on their arrival and is affordable and sustainable.- The Recipient will ensure that the accommodation is furnished appropriately.- The Recipient will meet and greet arriving refugees from the airport and escort them to their accommodation, providing a welcome pack of groceries at their home.- The Recipient will provide an initial cash allowance for each Beneficiary of £200  this is to ensure they have sufficient funds to live on while their claim for benefits is being processed. An additional payment of up to £100 per person may also be paid to local authorities where Universal Credit has been rolled out to cover initial delays in UC payments- The Recipient should ensure that Beneficiaries are provided with a dedicated source of advice and support to assist with registering for mainstream benefits and services, and signposting to other advice and information giving agencies  this support includes:- Assisting with registration for and collection of Biometric Residence Permits following arrival- Registering with local schools, English language and literacy classes- Attending local Job Centre Plus appointments for benefit assessments- Registering with a local GP- Advice around and referral to appropriate mental health services and to specialist services for victims of torture as appropriate- Providing assistance with access to employment.- The Recipient shall undertake an assessment with each Beneficiary of their English language capability to determine appropriate support arrangements through provision of English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) or equivalent. The purpose of the language tuition is to ensure that each Beneficiary is able to carry out basic transactions within the communities in which they have been placed. Beneficiaries should be able to access such classes within one month of their arrival and they should be made available until such time as suitable mainstream provision becomes available or until 12 months after arrival (whichever is sooner).

column3: As a user-led organisation, the exact focus of the Speak Up group will be determined by its members. But we expect the project to build the skills and confidence of women with learning disabilities in a number of ways. Women with learning disabilities will: - increase their confidence and self esteem; - increase their understanding of womens health; - improve their health seeking behaviour; - increase their social networks. While we have selected what we believe to be the priority that best matches out project, we do expect to have an impact across all three areas. Working alongside members of the Speak Up group, our staff will raise issues with local partners in order to improve outcomes. We anticipate this would focus on a broad range of issues, but health is likely to be a primary concern. As a result, we would expect, for example, to work with local nursing teams to increase the number of members accessing screenings. However, all such actions will be directed by the group and unexpected outcomes are likely.

column2: M.O.A.T - Coaching for the management of anxiety and recovery of trauma.
column3: Bus Stop Club, Ferndown - a grass roots befriending charity for those in crisis living in East Dorset and beyond. M.O.A.T. will offer a programme of individual coaching sessions to those experiencing high levels of anxiety and stress, which may have increased due to the COVID 19 pandemic. The grant will be put towards the core costs of this new project. Coaching in anxiety management and trauma recovery will enable clients to manage their levels of anxiety better and improve their overall health and well being as a result. Sessions can be for 6 weeks, or for 12 weeks if trauma recovery is also required. We anticipate most clients, but not all, will sign up for both part 1 and part 2, We have, therefore, calculated our numbers on the 12 week option.

Future Roots uses farming and the countryside to support young people who are at risk of exclusion from school due to social, emotional and mental health (SEMH) needs and other challenges. We are applying to deliver therapeutic support to young people who have been bereaved due to coronavirus and other reasons. The grant would pay for additional staff time to run the project. The most significant difference the project will make will be to provide an outlet for young people to explore their emotions, reducing non-productive coping strategies and increasing both social and personal functioning so that they can re-engage with their learning.

column3:
"Dorset National Landscape wants to support a more diverse range of people to engage with their local heritage to help heritage thrive, be more resilient, valued and cared for now and into the future. To achieve this ambition, we will drive forward, support and coordinate the growth of a network of trained volunteer Nature Buddies embedded into existing heritage and health organisations. These buddies will provide personalised support to overcome barriers faced to engaging with heritage. Digital access improvements and content creation will see heritage opportunities bought to any setting for varying interests and abilities. Community grants will support capital access improvements, increasing the provision of local, relevant and enjoyable spaces for all to enjoy.  
Nature Buddies, along with the digital and capital access improvements, will be a long-lasting legacy built into the ecosystem of support for people accessing heritage. Heritage will become valued in people’s lives."

"The project will have two outcomes: to collect oral histories from people who were children in WW2 and to dramatise them with young people as a series of short audio dramas. 

Life for children in Dorset during the war was extraordinary, but their experiences are under-recorded. 1944: American troops in their tens of thousands arrive to prepare for D-Day. Tanks and Army vehicles fill every tree-lined street. Commandos scale cliffs by night and sleep in family homes by day. Working with young people from deprived areas, the project team will find people who were children in the war years and record their stories for the Dorset History Centre oral archive. 

This archive material will then be used to make a series of radio dramas for community radio, podcasts and displays. Installed as part of a Nothe Fort exhibition, today's children will be the dramatised voices of young people during WW2."

"This project will commemorate 250 years since the birth of Jane Austen, connecting new audiences with her life and work and in particular, the important connections to Dorset.

Through an exhibition, workshops, school and community outputs, volunteer research projects and a public programme of events and activities, we will explore the role of Dorset within the novels, personal connections between Jane Austen and the County, as well as how this remains relevant for all of us today.

The legacy of this project will be new digital content including an online exhibition on our website and new items added to the online collections database.  We will also continue to provide related resources and workshops for schools, community groups and families as part of our ongoing programme.

We will also develop a new partnership with Jane Austen House that will include collaborative marketing and a shared talks programme."

"Lyme Regis Town Mill is a working water mill restored in the 1990’s run by volunteers and producing stone grown flour, providing workspaces for small businesses and the Malthouse, an arts/community space. Following a Lottery funded 2021 independent appraisal we want to provide new activities and inclusive opportunities for local organisations and individuals, who have already indicated support, recruit new volunteers and continue the mill's 'free to visit' model.
Our proposals will implement new interpretation and physical, artistic designed improvements, ensuring this heritage asset is preserved and sustainably enhanced, ensuring a high-quality presentation to visitors. The carbon reduction projects will generate free electricity and improved efficiency of the mill's hydro-electric unit. 
They will also enhance community well-being, benefit the local economy, and provide new volunteering and engagement opportunities for marginalised groups and individuals. The financial resilience of the Trust and the artisan-based makers at the site will be improved."

column2: "Plantlife Ryewater Farm Nature Reserve extension - Land purchase and establishment for conservation"
column3: "This project will allow Plantlife to expand one of its core grasslands nature reserves by acquiring an adjacent area of 1.8ha. This purchase, the associated initial capital works and our long-term commitment to its future management will allow us to bring this land into favourable condition. We will be able to directly contribute to restoring England’s species rich grassland. Acquisition of this extension to our existing reserve at Ryewater Farm is a cost-effective and efficient way to extend appropriate management. This land is within the same SSSI and can be classified as the same grassland habitat to that of Ryewater Farm. Plantlife’s acquisition of this land would offer potential for grassland recovery, improving and enhancing it to the same standard as that of the land already in the charity’s management. This project will extend the area that can be used for access and engagement activities in the future."

column3: "Having established a Youth Panel during the Test phase, Butterfly Conservation (BC) enters the ‘Grow’ phase in a stronger position to tackle our workforce challenge: the under-representation of young people (14-25 years of age) among our volunteers. The Youth Panel will lead our approach to the engagement of young people, tackling how to involve them in our work through new volunteering opportunities and how to retain their interest and support. Having tested different ways of working with our Panel and now understanding the processes we need to underpin this work, we are poised to implement the actions identified by the Panel. The legacy of this project will be the permanent fixture of a Youth Panel within the organisation, new ways of working for our staff and a growing and thriving (and increasingly diverse) young volunteer workforce that bolsters our ability to deliver our strategic aims."

column2: "ST THOMAS'S CHURCH MELBURY ABBAS ROOF REPLACEMENT"
column3: "The church roof is covered with clay tiles. The tiles on the southern aspects of the roof are in reasonable condition but many of the tiles on the northern aspects of the roof have degraded significantly. Clay tiles are particularly vulnerable to frost damage on north facing roof slopes. Over past decades, it has been possible to replace individual damaged tiles but now so many are damaged that this is no longer sensible or cost effective. Both the most recent Quinquennial Reviews [in 2015 and 2020) have recommended that the north facing parts of the roof be stripped and the tiles replaced. Our project aim is to replace the northern aspects of the church roof and keep the buckets out of St Thomas's!"

column2: "Dorset Museum & Art Gallery roof replacement and reimagining of Victorian Hall"
column3: "This project would replace the roof of the Victorian Hall and enable collections currently in storage, to be on public display.  We will be able to again tell the local story of Dorchester and the significance of the origins of Dorset Museum & Art Gallery.  We know our local audiences are disengaged with Museum, many no longer visiting, as this element had to be removed from the previous large capital project, due to escalating costs.  The roof also covers the library that includes many rare books, and staff offices.  All of these areas will be better protected, environmentally sustainability will improve and our running costs will be reduced due to improved performance of the building. column2: "St. Bartholomew's Church, Dorset - Owen Jones Wall Paintings Restoration"
column3:
"This project for St. Bartholomew's Church, Sutton Waldron, Dorset. It's purpose is the restoration and repair of the interior wall paintings and extending their awareness across all society. They were designed by Owen Jones - influential design theorist of the 19th century, seminal publisher of The Grammar of Ornament, interior designer of the 1851 Great Exhibition, pivotal creator of the Victoria and Albert Museum. Our polychromatic decorations are of major national importance. Originally completed in 1847, it is probably the only example of Jones' designs prior to their use in The Great Exhibition. It is also the last surviving example of a complete Jones' church interior.
The work required, determined by an exhaustive evaluation process, consists of:
Eliminating cause of damp in the west end of the church (tower area).
Restoring decorations affected by the damp and elapsed time,
Restoring ancillary paintwork affected by the damp and wear and tear."

column2: "How to Become A Peregrine - Exploring the Legacy of JA Baker's The Peregrine"
column3:
"Our organisation with 30 young people from deprived and rural wards in Dorset bring to life the pioneering field study and writing of disabled ornithologist/ conservationist JA Baker on the centenary of his birth in 1926. 
Collaborative workshops lead to a digital legacy of Baker’s seminal text - The Peregrine (1967) including 4 large scale illustrated montage panels depicting scenes from the book to be showcased at our Winter shows in 2025 with prints donated to University of Essex and Durlston Country Park for posterity. A digital legacy includes a webpage of the panels and a film of the workshop participants contributing to the illustrated panels and to a live score. Produced by award-winning BBC producer Sarah Cuddon and director of Cabinet of Living Cinema, Kieron Chissik, this legacy project celebrates Baker's groundbreaking nature writing and invites young people to be enthralled by nature writing, birdlife and green spaces."

"Nature Connection North Dorset will inspire a transformative shift in how communities across north Dorset connect with and care for their natural heritage. Through this flagship project, Dorset Wildlife Trust will empower residents to lead local nature recovery efforts, revitalising wild places, enhancing biodiversity, and deepening public engagement with nature. Over five years, we will deliver hands-on support, training, and community-led grants to help people restore woodlands, wetlands, and green spaces, especially in this nature-depleted area. This project will not only deliver visible environmental improvements but also foster stronger, healthier communities with lasting ties to their natural environment. The legacy we seek is a vibrant, connected network of people and places where nature is valued, nurtured, and sustained. By building capacity and embedding inclusive practices, this project will leave a long-term impact on both people and place, contributing to a more resilient and nature-rich future for north Dorset."

column2: "Flax Forward - From land to linen and beyond - Telling the story of a plant, a town and a landscape."
column3:
"This community-led project will celebrate Bridport’s flax-growing heritage while exploring the potential of locally grown, natural materials for a sustainable future.
The project will seek out, gather and collate knowledge from heritage collections, archives and a wide range of community sources. Kickstarted through a community research phase we will uncover lost flax infrastructure, memories, and oral histories. Adding to heritage data and making the story of Flax in the Bridport Area more accessible. 
Alongside community research we will provide hands-on, practical education in the cultivation and processing of flax. Community volunteers will work together to design and make a “Bridport Dress” using locally grown and processed Flax. 
Exhibitions and events will celebrate heritage and share it with wider audiences. By combining practical craft with heritage research and creative interpretation, the project will strengthen connections between people and their town highlighting how understanding the past can inspire the present."

column2: "Dorset History Centre: Past Lives, Future Proofed"
column3: "There has never been a more pressing need for the trusted, authentic voice provided by evidence and lived experience. This £5.6 million project will transform Dorset History Centre into a sustainable, inclusive, and nationally significant archive service. A new repository will secure the long-term preservation of Dorset’s documentary heritage for at least 30 years, while reconfigured and modernised public areas will enhance access, visitor experience, and operational efficiency. The project will deliver a strategic programme to widen participation and representation, initially through partnership with arts and heritage organisations and working with grass-roots organisations representing marginalised communities. Enhanced access to 200 years of Dorset’s extensive Quarter Session court rolls dating from 1709 will open up a major historical resource, while DHC will lead regional knowledge exchange in digital preservation and oral history. Together, these investments will strengthen Dorset’s cultural infrastructure, extend community engagement, and ensure resilient stewardship of the county’s heritage."

column2: "Bridging the Gap: Making Swanage Railway fit for the future."
column3:
"Swanage Railway has limited accessibility to its carriages for visitors who are wheelchair users or who have other physical disabilities and issues. We currently have a wagon that has been adapted which can be accessed by a ramp, but this does not provide equality of access or experience, and lack of seats means that those travelling in groups have to be separated on occasions. 

As well as accessibility for our public services, a learning and community engagement programme is being developed and for its successful delivery, it is essential that we have accessible carriages for visitors available at all times as well as for special events and projects. 
Swanage Railway is committed to consulting and engaging with disabled communities in Purbeck and wider Dorset in new, creative and innovative ways which this project funding will allow us to fulfil."

"Through this project, the Museum of East Dorset will become a more resilient, sustainable and inclusive organisation, better able to care for the heritage of East Dorset's people, villages and towns. We’ll deliver a diversified Fundraising Plan, modernise back-office digital systems, install solar PV and removable secondary glazing to cut carbon and running costs, and recruit a Community Engagement Manager to reach the most vulnerable in our community: isolated older residents, families on low incomes, and those underserved by heritage.

The project underpins our new three-year Business Plan, creating a financially and environmentally sustainable museum with diverse audiences, lower operating costs, increased fundraising income, and the organisational capacity to protect our local heritage long-term.

The project’s legacy will be a vibrant museum deeply rooted in its community, with the resilience to flourish despite the challenging external environment and trusted as a place where local heritage drives wellbeing, learning and pride."

column3: The Basic Payment Scheme makes payments to eligible farmers based on the amount of land being used for agricultural production and the equivalent number of payment entitlements held. The main payments are made at a flat rate per hectare of land / entitlement. Additional payments are made for meeting Greening requirements (Agricultural Practices Beneficial for the Climate and the Environment) and to Young Farmers (under 40 years of age). The Greening requirements vary depending on circumstances, but all farmers must also meet Cross Compliance requirements. These rules enforce laws around animal and plant health and sustainable agricultural practices. The scheme supports income in the agricultural sector, encourages younger people to take up farming and delivers environmental benefits and controls. RPA administers scheme for England and land in cross-border areas.Sub-outcome 1.7

column2: GCA PROG DEL RPA COUNTRYSIDE STEWARDSHIP
column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column2: GCA PROG DEL RPA COUNTRYSIDE STEWARDSHIP
column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column2: GCA PROG DEL RPA COUNTRYSIDE STEWARDSHIP
column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column3: Environmental Stewardship is an agri-environment scheme helping to:Improve water quality and reduce soil erosion by encouraging management which can help to meet these aims;Improve conditions for farmland wildlife including birds, mammals, butterflies and bees;Maintain and enhance landscape character by helping to maintain important features such as traditional field boundaries;Protect the historic environment including archaeological features and artefacts.The scheme, which replaces the older Countryside Stewardship and Environmentally Sensitive Area schemes, is composed of two levels: the Entry Level Stewardship (ELS), Organic Entry Level Stewardship (OELS) for Organic farms, Upland Entry Level Stewardship (UELS) comprising the lower levels; and the Higher Level Stewardship (HLS) for the upper level.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 - Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column2: Afghan Citizen Resettlement Scheme & Relocation and Assistance Policy
column3: This grant will fund the provision of humanitarian protection to those people who qualify under:The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS), which provides those put at risk by recent events in Afghanistan with a route to safety. This scheme will prioritise:(i) those who have assisted the UK efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such as democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law (for example, judges, womens rights activists, academics, journalists); and(ii) vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk, and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT).This scheme will resettle up to 20,000 people at risk, with 5,000 in the first year. Spouses, partners, and dependent children, under the age of 18, of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk because of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.

The Safer Streets Fund allows police, local authorities and civil society organisations to invest in crime prevention initiatives across England and Wales to reduce and prevent neighbourhood crime (NC), violence against women and girls (VAWG) and anti-social behaviour (ASB) in areas that receive funding making communities (residents and businesses) safer and reducing demand on the police.

This Funding is available to participating Recipients in the UK (principally, but not exclusively, Clinical Commissioning Groups) in respect of healthcare expenditure incurred supporting Refugees brought to the UK under the UKs resettlement schemes. Recipients are encouraged to share their learning of how to best manage the complex health and wellbeing needs of refugees with other participating Recipients (usually Clinical Commissioning Groups, but local and regional authorities can also be included) to help support the integration of refugees in the UK.

Funding will ensure Dorset Police have suitable and safe marine vessels to patrol waters in the Southwest of the UK. Working alongside Border Force, these new vessels will provide a robust deterrent to those looking to exploit the English Channel for illegal immigration, but also drugs or firearms. Dorset Police have also indicated that the purchase of these two vessels will improve the current capability exponentially, ensuring officers can patrol their responsible areas and support maritime policing to neighbouring forces. They will also be able to respond to other maritime-linked crimes such as theft, anti-social behaviour and terrorism.

The aim of the grant scheme is to reduce levels of serious violence and ASB, thus contributing to key strategic priorities of cutting crime. We will achieve this through the funding allocated to PCCs to undertake targeted, data driven hotspot patrolling, which may be supplemented by Problem Oriented Policing (POP). POP also known as problem-solving policing is an approach to develop targeted area bespoke interventions which to prevent and reduce crime and disorder.

column2: Afghan Resettlement, Relocation and Integration Support Programme
column3: Local authorities are the main recipients of grant funding in support of those who have been accepted for resettlement and relocation under the Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS) and Afghan Relocation and Assistance Policy (ARAP). Local authority support under these schemes is voluntary and those who agree to support new arrivals to the UK from 01 March 2025 are required to provide time limited integration support in transitional accommodation (up to 9 months) to support beneficiaries to find their own settled accommodation in the UK, develop their English language skills, build self-sufficiency skills and through support and signposting find employment. They will be funded for these activities. For those local authorities who agree to support individuals who settle in their local area, the local authority can claim further funding over the course of the next 3 years to help individuals integrate into communities and continue on their journey to self-sufficiency. This grant stream also includes additional payments, in the first year upon arrival in the UK, to support with education and the provision of healthcare services. The latter are made to Integrated Care Boards and other health bodies in the devolved administrations.

column2: GCA PROG DEL RPA COUNTRYSIDE STEWARDSHIP
column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-outcome 1.4

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-outcome 1.4

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-outcome 1.4

column3: 5G RuralDorset will deliver the following:Business models for rural 5G servicesWe will address the cost and design challenges of using common wireless infrastructure at national scale to deliver services to rural communities. This will be evaluated by three service providers and across four different test-beds that respond to the needs of those living, working and visiting rural and coastal regions of Dorset and beyond.Rural 5G Testbed rural communities are poorly serviced by wireless connectivity. We will deploy a wide-area 5G wireless testbed allowing businesses and academia to prove the sustainable commercial case for improved 5G connectivity in rural locations. We will deploy new wireless technology on existing masts and fibre owned and operated by internet service provider Wessex Internet allowing rapid deployment on a significant scale. The resulting connectivity will support uses in agriculture and provide access to digital services tackling rural issues including isolation and social care needs. This will show that existing and new infrastructure can be combined to deliver next generation connectivity more affordably.Connected Coast the UKs coastal regions generate significant economic wealth and support a range of leisure activities that boost health and well-being. But the coast can be very dangerous. There are serious challenges communicating in such regions, with the first responder community and organisations including the RNLI, Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) and General Lighthouse Authority (GLA) having very limited access to digital communications services. We will deploy a 5G services test-bed in the Lulworth Cove area and a further maritime safety test-bed on infrastructure along the coast. We will trial digital applications that engage with the public and improve the responsiveness of emergency services to incidents. We will evaluate the upgrade of existing infrastructure around the coast and develop the social and economic case for deployment, considering additional use cases from tourism and aquaculture to education and healthcare.5G Innovation Testbed We will deploy an advanced connectivity testbed at the heart of Dorset Innovation Park, a Local Enterprise Zone and advanced-engineering centre which already supports large and small companies that develop innovative connected products and services. This testbed will be connected to other sites in the UK and focus on wide-area connectivity solutions for rural and coastal regions. It will support businesses operating in the county and across the supply chain to test and develop products before deployment in a collaborative and secure way in this strategically important location.

column3: The NRHE to HERs project forms part of the Heritage Information Access Strategy (HIAS) which is a partnership programme led by Historic England on behalf of the sector. Principle 1 of this strategy states that Local Authority HERs should be the first point of call for and primary trusted source of investigative research data and knowledge. At the current time, heritage data is collected both through local authority HERs and the NRHE which differ in content, quality and standards resulting in the duplication of data. The project aims to rationalise historic environment data and records at national and local levels through the transfer of data from the NRHE to HERs which will make them available to a wider audience.

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.

column2: GRCF2021 The Axe Valley Oasis: bioresilience and environmental engagement
column3: We will contribute to all three objectives:1. Nature conservation and restorationCurrently, 10% of the site supports a huge diversity of wildlife, including 28 Natural England 's41' Priority Species and 25 Dorset Notable Species. We will transform the surrounding farmland into a species-rich mosaic of woodland, wetland, grassland and wood pasture, permanently maintained through a new conservation grazing regime. An impoverished stretch of the river Axe running through the site will be restored through brash sediment management, creating into a vibrant ecosystem.2. Nature-based solutions, particularly for climate change mitigation and adaptionThe project will sequester carbon in both living trees and wetland soils. Restoration of the River Axe will increase flooding on site, (brining habitat benefits to wading birds), and so reduce the risk of flooding downstream .3. Connecting people with natureOver 1000 people will be engaged in environmental educational and eco-therapeutic opportunities on site, using habitat restoration as a catalyst for change in their lives and behaviours.7 new jobs will be created - two permanent posts and 5 paid work placements for young people.Our project has been planned over the last 18 months and is ready for an immediate start.

column2: GRCF2021: Court Farm Rewilding Project - delivering nature's recovery and climate resilience
column3: Imagine being able to access a wilderness direct from your front door. Once barren fields, ringed with barbed wire, polluting the waterways and excluding the community, now a restored landscape, alive with returning wildlife, grazing animals and people.Dorset Wildlife Trust has a unique opportunity to establish a large community-based nature recovery project. We have created a new financial model using nature-based solutions to acquire 170ha of low-quality agricultural land in a key location. We will build a Nature Recovery Network in Dorset at a landscape-scale that will help control pollution entering the internationally important Poole Harbour while addressing the climate and ecological crises.The project will establish the UKs first community rewilding project, as well as the first such project in Dorset. We will rewild 150ha including 30ha of new wetlands that restore nature, hold back and cleanse water and capture carbon. The local community will help to create wild areas close to them, including 12.2ha of new community woodlands and orchards. The project will create two full-time jobs and support local contractors in delivering a range of nature-recovery activities.

column3: After four years of effort in Rockingham Forest, Butterfly Conservation has re-introduced the Chequered Skipper butterfly to England at a single site, demonstrating that it can work. We now need to secure this population in the landscape and enable the public to enjoy this conservation success story.This critical second phase of restoration will enhance woodland habitats and identify future management work through landscape planning. Improving the connectivity of open habitats will also benefit the Grizzled Skipper and Dingy Skipper in the same landscape.The release site for the Chequered Skipper has, to date, remained secret. Now is the right time to invite the public to visit the area with Skipper-sighting in mind, boosting local nature tourism. Rangers will connect people with nature, nurturing appreciation and understanding of Rockinghams butterflies and their conservation. They will encourage visitors to participate in wildlife surveys or become seasonal volunteer rangers.Work will take place in 19 locations. Third Party Agreements, felling licences and SSSI consents will be provided within four months of the start of the project.This project will support two existing members of Butterfly Conservation staff, two new rangers and engage with at least nine local contractors/consultants.

column3: The Water Environment Improvement Fund (WEIF) grant is to support the maintenance of partnerships across Englands catchments, primarily to deliver a catchment based approach to water, land and flood management. Partnerships need to consider the targets of the 25 year environment plan, including: clean and plentiful water, thriving plants and wildlife, using resources from nature more sustainably and efficiently, enhancing beauty, heritage and engagement with the natural environment and mitigating and adapting to climate change. This focus will include actions to deliver improvements to the Water Environment (Water Framework Directive) (England & Wales) Regulations 2017 objectives, climate crisis, biodiversity crisis, flood risk, coastal erosion, growing population, plastics and land management delivered through an integrated catchment approach. Managing the water environment (including rivers, lakes, groundwater, estuaries and the sea) can be very complex and requires balancing the priorities and needs of multiple water users, landowners, and organisations with differing roles and responsibilities considering how to maximise natural capital and net gain. Individual grant values range from £3,250 for sub-catchments to £250,000 for the Catchment Based Approach (CaBA) National Support Group (NSG).

column2: RPA FARMING INVESTMENT FUND (Farming Equipment and Technology Fund)
column3: The Farming Investment Fund comprises two different sub-schemes. column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.

Spouses, partners, and dependent children under the age of 18 of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk as a result of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.Plus British Nationals and their close family members relocated from Afghanistan to the UK by HM Government.There are currently approximately 15,000 people in the United Kingdom who will qualify under one of these schemes in this current financial year.

The VPRS scheme has been expanded to meet a commitment made by the former Prime Minister, and is being run by a tri-partite team of officials (the Syrian Resettlement Programme) from the the Home Office and the departments for International Development and Communities and Local Government. This team sits within the Resettlement, Asylum Support and Integration Direcorate in UK Visas and Immigration. This team also has responsibility for running the Vulnerable Childrens Resettlement Scheme.As such, this funding is to be used to meet a government commitment, rather than a Home Office strategic priority. Three key objectives have been set for the schemes: resettling Syrian refugees in a way that:Secures and Protects the vulnerable persons and the UK, andHas the Well-being of the vulnerable persons and the welcoming communities at the centre of decision making, andDelivers value for money for the UK tax payer.This grant is primarily designed to assist with promoting refugee well being, whilst ensuring value for money. It is designed to contribute to costs incurred for the first year that beneficiaries spend in the UK for primary and secondary health care costs.The VPR scheme was upscaled in September 2015 to meet commitments made by the former Prime Minister, including to resettle 1,000 Syrians by Christmas 2015. In view of the scale of the challenge and limited time available, the Home Secretary authorised the formation of a Gold Command Structure, which provided the designated Gold Commander (Paul Morrison) with high-level Ministerial authority to make the necessary funding and operational decisions to deliver these commitments. The VCRS scheme was announced in April 2016 and utilises the same delivery partners.Since then the formation of the Gold Command, the Programme  which operates both schemes  has had regular contact with Ministers at Secretary of State level. They are aware of our choice of delivery partners and funding model.The VPR and VCRS schemes are being evaluated through a programme of data monitoring and qualitative research and this will include examining some VFM considerations.

column3: 5G RuralDorset will deliver the following:Business models for rural 5G servicesWe will address the cost and design challenges of using common wireless infrastructure at national scale to deliver services to rural communities. This will be evaluated by three service providers and across four different test-beds that respond to the needs of those living, working and visiting rural and coastal regions of Dorset and beyond.Rural 5G Testbed rural communities are poorly serviced by wireless connectivity. We will deploy a wide-area 5G wireless testbed allowing businesses and academia to prove the sustainable commercial case for improved 5G connectivity in rural locations. We will deploy new wireless technology on existing masts and fibre owned and operated by internet service provider Wessex Internet allowing rapid deployment on a significant scale. The resulting connectivity will support uses in agriculture and provide access to digital services tackling rural issues including isolation and social care needs. This will show that existing and new infrastructure can be combined to deliver next generation connectivity more affordably.Connected Coast the UKs coastal regions generate significant economic wealth and support a range of leisure activities that boost health and well-being. But the coast can be very dangerous. There are serious challenges communicating in such regions, with the first responder community and organisations including the RNLI, Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) and General Lighthouse Authority (GLA) having very limited access to digital communications services. We will deploy a 5G services test-bed in the Lulworth Cove area and a further maritime safety test-bed on infrastructure along the coast. We will trial digital applications that engage with the public and improve the responsiveness of emergency services to incidents. We will evaluate the upgrade of existing infrastructure around the coast and develop the social and economic case for deployment, considering additional use cases from tourism and aquaculture to education and healthcare.5G Innovation Testbed We will deploy an advanced connectivity testbed at the heart of Dorset Innovation Park, a Local Enterprise Zone and advanced-engineering centre which already supports large and small companies that develop innovative connected products and services. This testbed will be connected to other sites in the UK and focus on wide-area connectivity solutions for rural and coastal regions. It will support businesses operating in the county and across the supply chain to test and develop products before deployment in a collaborative and secure way in this strategically important location.

column2: GRCF2021 The Axe Valley Oasis: bioresilience and environmental engagement
column3: We will contribute to all three objectives:1. Nature conservation and restorationCurrently, 10% of the site supports a huge diversity of wildlife, including 28 Natural England 's41' Priority Species and 25 Dorset Notable Species. We will transform the surrounding farmland into a species-rich mosaic of woodland, wetland, grassland and wood pasture, permanently maintained through a new conservation grazing regime. An impoverished stretch of the river Axe running through the site will be restored through brash sediment management, creating into a vibrant ecosystem.2. Nature-based solutions, particularly for climate change mitigation and adaptionThe project will sequester carbon in both living trees and wetland soils. Restoration of the River Axe will increase flooding on site, (brining habitat benefits to wading birds), and so reduce the risk of flooding downstream .3. Connecting people with natureOver 1000 people will be engaged in environmental educational and eco-therapeutic opportunities on site, using habitat restoration as a catalyst for change in their lives and behaviours.7 new jobs will be created - two permanent posts and 5 paid work placements for young people.Our project has been planned over the last 18 months and is ready for an immediate start.

column2: GRCF2021: Court Farm Rewilding Project - delivering nature's recovery and climate resilience
column3: Imagine being able to access a wilderness direct from your front door. Once barren fields, ringed with barbed wire, polluting the waterways and excluding the community, now a restored landscape, alive with returning wildlife, grazing animals and people.Dorset Wildlife Trust has a unique opportunity to establish a large community-based nature recovery project. We have created a new financial model using nature-based solutions to acquire 170ha of low-quality agricultural land in a key location. We will build a Nature Recovery Network in Dorset at a landscape-scale that will help control pollution entering the internationally important Poole Harbour while addressing the climate and ecological crises.The project will establish the UKs first community rewilding project, as well as the first such project in Dorset. We will rewild 150ha including 30ha of new wetlands that restore nature, hold back and cleanse water and capture carbon. The local community will help to create wild areas close to them, including 12.2ha of new community woodlands and orchards. The project will create two full-time jobs and support local contractors in delivering a range of nature-recovery activities.

column3: After four years of effort in Rockingham Forest, Butterfly Conservation has re-introduced the Chequered Skipper butterfly to England at a single site, demonstrating that it can work. We now need to secure this population in the landscape and enable the public to enjoy this conservation success story.This critical second phase of restoration will enhance woodland habitats and identify future management work through landscape planning. Improving the connectivity of open habitats will also benefit the Grizzled Skipper and Dingy Skipper in the same landscape.The release site for the Chequered Skipper has, to date, remained secret. Now is the right time to invite the public to visit the area with Skipper-sighting in mind, boosting local nature tourism. Rangers will connect people with nature, nurturing appreciation and understanding of Rockinghams butterflies and their conservation. They will encourage visitors to participate in wildlife surveys or become seasonal volunteer rangers.Work will take place in 19 locations. Third Party Agreements, felling licences and SSSI consents will be provided within four months of the start of the project.This project will support two existing members of Butterfly Conservation staff, two new rangers and engage with at least nine local contractors/consultants.

column2: M11 - Agri-environment- Organic Farming Exchq funded NSA P2
column3: This measure covers Agri-environment-organic farming support. Payments are based on income foregone and, where relevant, additional costs resulting from converting to an organic farming system. There are 5 different conversion payments available for different farming systems: Rotational Land; Improved Permanent Pasture; Unimproved Permanent Pasture; Horticulture; and Top Fruit. This measure aims to fund organic conversion and maintenance by active farmers and builds on existing conversion and maintenance support under the previous RD programme Environmental Stewardship (Organic Higher Level and Entry Level Stewardship) elements. Activities funded under this measure support farmers wishing to convert to and maintain organic farming systems for environmental benefits. Investments contribute to meeting Englands Biodiversity 2020 goals and legal obligations under the Habitats and Species and Water Framework Directives. Support also aims to deliver the main objectives on biodiversity and the water environment (including flood management). RPA administers for measures in England.

Payments are based on income foregone and, where relevant, additional costs resulting from converting to an organic farming system. There are 5 different conversion payments available for different farming systems: Rotational Land; Improved Permanent Pasture; Unimproved Permanent Pasture; Horticulture; and Top Fruit. This measure aims to fund organic conversion and maintenance by active farmers and builds on existing conversion and maintenance support under the previous RD programme Environmental Stewardship (Organic Higher Level and Entry Level Stewardship) elements. Activities funded under this measure support farmers wishing to convert to and maintain organic farming systems for environmental benefits. Investments contribute to meeting Englands Biodiversity 2020 goals and legal obligations under the Habitats and Species and Water Framework Directives. Support also aims to deliver the main objectives on biodiversity and the water environment (including flood management). RPA administers for measures in England.

column2: M15 - Forest environmental and climate services and forest conservation Exchq funded NSA P2
column3: This measure covers grants for Co-operation under Countryside Productivity, Countryside Stewardship and ESIF Growth Programme to micro and small enterprises, farmers and foresters engaged in cooperative activities. This measure encourages and promotes a range of cooperative activity which encourages farmers, forest holders, private businesses and public bodies, or participants in supply chains to work together to take forward priorities for investment and overcome disadvantages of fragmentation. The measure develops priorities in environment, climate change and biodiversity; supporting farmers and foresters to improve supply chains or develop short supply chains; develop initiatives to tackle animal health and welfare issues; as well as cooperation between public bodies and private businesses to develop the rural economy. Local co-operation in tourism activities are supported that improve the attractiveness of the overall destination, help develop the supply chain in the visitor economy and encourage collaborative activity or pilot projects developing agri-food hubs or clusters in particular geographic areas. This measure will be used to implement the European Innovation Partnership for agricultural productivity and sustainability. RPA administers for measures in England

Ministers have agreed to allocate £75.6m from the 20/21 Police Settlement to complete and close-down police-led programmes that require an additional years funding (due to slippage) to support delivery of planned benefits and outcomes. Continuing programmes will also receive additional funding for growth areas to include Digital Workforce, uplift in Police ICT, and Digital Forensics. These have been allocated to support delivery of Ministerial priorities linked to the recruitment of 20k Police officers.The continuing programmes were previously funded through the Police Transformation Fund (PTF), which closed on 31 March 2020. This was communicated as part of a Written Ministerial Statement, laid to Parliament on 23rd January detailing the final Police Settlement for 2020/21.What this grant covers:The allocation will complete the roll out of Single Online Home (policing website), further develop national data analytics, help to establish a central contracting authority for Police ICT, progress digital transfer of communications with CJS partners, maintain portfolio capability to programmes and support governance reform, which includes the development of a Strategic Change and Investment Board (SCIB).
